Search by meaning

Embeddings, cosine similarity, chunks and recall@k, by hand.

🧭 Search by meaning

A keyword search finds the texts that contain the words of the question. Ask “How do I get my money back?” and it can miss the page “Refund policy”: the two have no word in common.

An embedding model turns a whole text (a question, a paragraph, a page) into one vector: its embedding. It is trained so that texts with a similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions, even when they share no words.

That gives search by meaning (semantic search). Store the embeddings of your documents. For each question (the query), compute its embedding and take the documents whose vectors are nearest to it. “Nearest” usually means the highest cosine similarity: the dot product divided by the two lengths.

cos(a, b) = a·b / (|a|·|b|)
a·b = a₁·b₁ + a₂·b₂
|a| = √(a₁² + a₂²)
cos = 1: same direction; cos = 0: right angle

The formulas are written for vectors of two numbers: enough to work everything out by hand. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of numbers (the sums just get longer), and a short text gets as many as a long one.

Task. A query has the embedding q = (3, 4), and a document has the embedding d1 = (4, 3). What is their cosine similarity?

Show the solution

The dot product is 3·4 + 4·3 = 24. Both lengths are √(9 + 16) = 5, so the cosine is 24 / (5·5) = 24 / 25 = 0.96. That is close to 1: the vectors point in almost the same direction, so for the model the two texts are close in meaning.

Task. A query has the embedding (3, 4), and a document has the embedding (−4, 3). What is their cosine similarity?

Show the solution

The dot product is 3·(−4) + 4·3 = −12 + 12 = 0, so the cosine is 0 whatever the lengths are. The two vectors are at a right angle: for the model that made them, the query and the document have nothing in common.

Task. A document has the embedding d3 = (6, 8): the query q = (3, 4) with every number doubled. What is their cosine similarity?

Show the answer

Right answer: 1: the cosine compares directions, and they are the same

(3·6 + 4·8) / (5·10) = 50 / 50 = 1. Doubling changes the length of a vector, not its direction, and the cosine does not depend on the length: its formula divides by the lengths. It can never be above 1. Many embedding models already return vectors of length 1: then the cosine is simply the dot product.

Task. The query is q = (3, 4). Rank the four documents by their cosine similarity to it, from the highest to the lowest.

Show the solution
  1. d3 = (6, 8)
  2. d1 = (4, 3)
  3. d4 = (0, 5)
  4. d2 = (−4, 3)

For d4: (3·0 + 4·5) / (5·5) = 20 / 25 = 0.8. So the cosines are 1 for d3, 0.96 for d1, 0.8 for d4 and 0 for d2. A search needs only this order: it returns the documents from the top of the list. The values themselves differ from model to model, so compare only cosines that come from the same model.

✂️ What you store: chunks

An embedding is one vector for a whole text. For a long manual it would be a blur of all its topics, and it would fit no single question well. So a long document is first cut into chunks: pieces that are usually a few hundred tokens long, each with its own embedding.

The search then returns chunks, not whole documents. The best ones are later passed to a language model together with the question: the next step of your path shows how.

The size is a compromise. A chunk that is too big mixes several topics in one vector, and only a few such chunks fit into the context window. A chunk that is too small loses the sentences around it that give it meaning. A small overlap between neighbours helps: a thought cut at a border can stay whole in one of them.

Embedding models have an input limit too: a text that is longer is cut off or refused. That is one more reason to cut documents into chunks.

Task. A manual of 12,000 tokens is cut into chunks of 500 tokens, without overlap. How many chunks are there?

Show the solution

12,000 / 500 = 24 chunks, so the manual gets 24 embeddings and not one. With an overlap there would be more chunks, because each of them would repeat a part of its neighbour.

Task. For search by meaning, a long document is first cut into chunks, and each chunk gets its own embedding. Why not one embedding for the whole document?

Show the answer

Right answer: One vector blurs the document's many topics, and small chunks fit into a model's context window

An embedding has as many numbers for a long text as for a short one. For a long document it becomes a kind of average of many topics and fits no single question well. A chunk is usually about one thing, and the few best chunks fit into the context window of the language model that writes the answer.

🎯 The top k, and how to measure a search

A search by meaning returns the k chunks with the highest cosine: the top k. You choose k, for example 5. The search returns them even when none of them holds the answer, so it has to be measured.

Collect real questions, and for each one mark by hand the chunks that hold its answer: the relevant chunks. Recall@k is the share of the relevant chunks that the search puts into its top k.

Work it out for every test question and take the average. Now you can compare two embedding models or two kinds of search on your own data, and you do not have to guess. And remember: what the search misses, the language model never sees.

recall@k = relevant in the top k / all relevant

It is the recall you may know from classifiers: here the search “flags” its first k results.

Task. A search runs over a collection of text chunks. For one question, 4 chunks are relevant: they hold the answer. The top 5 results contain 3 of them. What is recall@5? Answer with a number from 0 to 1.

Show the solution

3 of the 4 relevant chunks were found: 3 / 4 = 0.75. Recall divides by the number of relevant chunks, not by the number of results: 3 / 5 = 0.6 is another measure, precision@5, the share of the results that are relevant. One relevant chunk in four was missed: a language model that gets only the top 5 never sees it.

Task. A user searches the documentation for the exact error code E4012. Which kind of search usually finds it more reliably?

Show the answer

Right answer: A keyword search: it looks for this exact string of characters

A code has almost no meaning for an embedding to hold: for the model E4012 and E4013 can look nearly the same, so the nearest chunks may be about other errors. A keyword search matches the exact string. Many systems run both kinds of search and merge the results: this is called hybrid search.

Task. An embedding model gives two texts a cosine similarity of 0.95. What does that tell you?

Show the answer

Right answer: For the model they are close in meaning, but that says nothing about whether they are true

A high cosine says that the two vectors point almost the same way: for the model, the texts are about the same thing. It is not a share of common words, not proof of copying and not a measure of truth. “The guarantee lasts 2 years” and “The guarantee lasts 3 years” can have a very high cosine, but at most one of them is right.

Remember

  • An embedding model turns a text into a vector. The cosine similarity compares directions, not lengths, and a high cosine means “similar for the model”, not “true”.
  • Long documents are stored as chunks, each with its own embedding. A chunk that is too big blurs several topics; one that is too small loses its meaning.
  • Measure a search with recall@k: the share of the relevant chunks that reach the top k. Work it out on real questions whose relevant chunks you have marked.
  • A keyword search usually finds exact strings such as error codes more reliably, so real systems often combine both kinds: hybrid search.
